title: Book Three (1805) — Chapter 8
paragraphs: The day after Rostov's visit to Boris, a review was held of the Austrian and Russian forces — both the fresh troops from Russia and those who had been campaigning under Kutuzov. The two Emperors — the Russian Emperor with his heir the Tsarevich, and the Austrian Emperor with the Archduke — inspected the combined allied army of eighty thousand men.

From early morning, the immaculate troops had been on the move, forming up on the field before the fortress. Thousands of boots and bayonets marched and halted at officers' commands, turned with banners flying, formed up at intervals, and wheeled around similar blocks of infantry in different uniforms. Then came the rhythmic beat of hooves and the jingling of gleaming cavalry in blue, red, and green braided uniforms, led by smartly dressed bandsmen on black, bay, and gray horses. After them, rattling and gleaming, came the artillery — polished cannons quivering on their carriages, trailing the smell of burning match — which rolled between the infantry and cavalry to take up its assigned position. Not just the generals in full-dress uniforms, their waists cinched tight (whether thin or thick), red necks squeezed into stiff collars, wearing sashes and every decoration they owned — not just the polished, pomaded officers — but every single soldier with his freshly washed and shaven face, his weapons cleaned and polished to a shine, every horse groomed until its coat gleamed like satin with each hair of its dampened mane lying perfectly smooth — all of them sensed that this was no small matter but something important and solemn. Every general and every soldier felt his own insignificance, understood that he was merely a drop in that ocean of men, yet at the same time felt his strength as part of that enormous whole.

From early morning, intense effort and activity had been under way, and by ten o'clock everything was in perfect order. The ranks stretched across the vast field. The entire army was arranged in three lines: cavalry in front, artillery behind it, and infantry at the rear.

A gap like a street was left between each pair of lines. The three parts of the army were clearly distinct: Kutuzov's battle-tested troops (with the Pavlograds on the right flank of the front line), the recently arrived forces from Russia — both Guards and line regiments — and the Austrian troops. But they all stood in the same formation, under a single command, in uniform order.
An excited whisper rippled through the ranks like wind through leaves: "They're coming! They're coming!" Anxious voices rang out, and a final wave of preparation swept through all the troops.

A group appeared approaching from the direction of Olmutz. And at that moment, though the day was calm, a light breeze passed over the army, just barely stirring the streamers on the lances and ruffling the unfurled standards against their staffs. It was as if the army itself, with that slight flutter, was expressing its joy at the Emperors' approach. A single voice rang out: "Eyes front!" Then, like roosters crowing at dawn, the command was repeated from all directions, and everything fell silent.

In the deathly stillness, only the tramping of horses could be heard. This was the Emperors' entourage. They rode up to the flank, and the trumpets of the first cavalry regiment played the general march. It seemed as though the trumpeters weren't playing at all — as though the army itself, overjoyed at the Emperors' approach, had spontaneously burst into music. Through these sounds, only one voice could be clearly heard: the young, warm voice of Emperor Alexander. He spoke the words of greeting, and the first regiment roared "Hurrah!" so thunderously, so continuously, so joyfully that the soldiers themselves were awed by their own numbers and the immensity of their combined power.

Rostov, standing in the front ranks of Kutuzov's army — which the Tsar approached first — felt exactly what every other man in that army felt: a sense of losing himself, a proud awareness of collective might, and a passionate devotion to the man who had caused this triumph.

He felt that a single word from that man would send this entire vast mass — and he himself, an insignificant speck within it — through fire and water, to commit any act, to die, or to perform the greatest heroism. And so he couldn't help trembling, his heart stopping at the thought that the word might come at any moment.

"Hurrah! Hurrah! Hurrah!" roared from every side as regiment after regiment greeted the Tsar with the strains of the march, then another "Hurrah!" The general march, then "Hurrah! Hurrah!" — growing ever louder and fuller, merging into a single deafening roar.

Until the Tsar reached a given regiment, it stood in silence and stillness like a lifeless body. But the moment he drew near, it burst to life, its thunder joining the roar of the whole line he had already passed. Through the terrible, deafening wall of sound, amid the motionless square formations standing rigid as stone, hundreds of riders in the imperial retinue moved casually but gracefully, and above all freely. And at the head of them rode two men — the Emperors. On them was focused the total, intense, passionate attention of that entire mass of humanity.
The handsome young Emperor Alexander, wearing the uniform of the Horse Guards and a cocked hat with its peaks front and back, drew every eye with his pleasant face and clear, resonant voice.

Rostov was not far from the trumpeters, and with his sharp eyesight he recognized the Tsar and watched his approach. When Alexander was about twenty paces away and Nicholas could clearly make out every feature of his handsome, happy young face, he was swept by a feeling of tenderness and rapture unlike anything he had ever known. Every expression, every movement of the Tsar's seemed enchanting to him.
As the Tsar stopped in front of the Pavlograds, he said something in French to the Austrian Emperor and smiled.

Seeing that smile, Rostov couldn't help smiling himself, feeling an even stronger surge of love for his sovereign. He longed to express that love somehow, and knowing it was impossible, he was ready to weep. The Tsar called the regiment's colonel over and said a few words to him.
"Oh God, what would happen to me if the Emperor spoke to me?" Rostov thought. "I would die of happiness!"

The Tsar addressed the officers as well: "I thank you all, gentlemen. I thank you with my whole heart." To Rostov, every word sounded like a voice from heaven. How gladly he would have died on the spot for his Tsar!
"You have earned the St. George's standards and will prove worthy of them."
"Oh, to die, to die for him," Rostov thought.
The Tsar said something more that Rostov couldn't hear, and the soldiers, straining their lungs, shouted "Hurrah!"
Rostov too, bending over his saddle, bellowed "Hurrah!" with every ounce of strength, feeling he could injure himself with that shout if it meant fully expressing his devotion.
The Tsar paused for a few moments in front of the hussars, as if unsure of something.
"How can the Emperor be uncertain?" Rostov thought — but even this hesitation seemed majestic and enchanting, like everything else the Tsar did.

The hesitation lasted only an instant. The Tsar's foot, in the narrow, pointed boot that was fashionable at the time, touched the flank of the bob-tailed bay mare he rode. His white-gloved hand gathered the reins, and he moved off, accompanied by an irregularly swaying crowd of aides-de-camp. Farther and farther he rode, stopping at other regiments, until finally only his white plumes were visible to Rostov among the entourage surrounding the Emperors.

Among the riders in the retinue, Rostov spotted Bolkonsky, sitting his horse with casual indifference. He remembered their clash the day before, and the question arose: should he challenge Bolkonsky or not? "Of course not!" he thought now. "How can I even consider it at a moment like this? At a time of such love, such ecstasy, such self-sacrifice, what do any of our petty quarrels and insults matter? I love and forgive everyone now."

When the Emperor had passed nearly all the regiments, the troops began the ceremonial march past him. Rostov rode by on Bedouin — the horse he'd recently bought from Denisov — at the rear of his squadron, which meant he was riding alone and in full view of the Emperor.

As he approached, Rostov — an excellent horseman — spurred Bedouin twice and put him into the showy, collected trot the horse adopted when excited. With his foaming muzzle tucked to his chest and tail streaming out behind him, Bedouin seemed to feel the Emperor's gaze upon him too. He moved magnificently, lifting his hooves high in an elegant, floating action, as if barely touching the ground.

Rostov himself, legs pressed well back, stomach drawn in, feeling himself and his horse as one, rode past the Emperor with a fierce but blissful expression on his face — "like a real devil," as Denisov would have put it.
"Fine fellows, the Pavlograds!" the Emperor remarked.
"My God, how happy I would be if he ordered me to ride into fire this very second!" Rostov thought.

When the review was over, the newly arrived officers and Kutuzov's veterans alike gathered in groups to discuss the awards, the Austrian uniforms and formations, and Bonaparte — and how badly things would go for him now, especially once the Essen corps arrived and Prussia joined their side.
But in every group, the main topic of conversation was Emperor Alexander. Every word he'd spoken, every gesture he'd made was described with adoration.

Everyone shared a single wish: to advance against the enemy as soon as possible under the Emperor's personal command. With the Emperor himself leading them, they could not possibly lose to anyone — so believed Rostov and most of the officers after the review.
All of them felt more confident of victory than they would have after winning two actual battles.
